title: Health impacts of water risks through water-borne and vector-borne diseases in informal settlements in the Global South and India
headline: Water risks drive health crises in informal areas
bullets: Synthesized evidence on water risks and diseases in informal settlements

plain.question: How do water risks affect health in informal city areas?
plain.method: A literature review of studies on water and health in informal settlements.
plain.finding: Poor water, floods, and bad sanitation cause high rates of water and vector diseases.
plain.why: It shows that fixing health needs better water, drainage, and local governance.

full.explainer: Informal city settlements face major water risks that hurt people's health and daily lives. This review looks at how problems like water scarcity, dirty water, floods, and weak infrastructure combine to spread diseases in these communities. The authors explain that water risk is not just about missing water pipes. Instead, danger is created when intermittent water service, unsafe water storage, exposed wastewater, poor drainage, and hazard-prone locations all happen at the same time. These bad conditions lead to diseases spread by waste, mosquito bites, and contact with dirty water, alongside stress and economic loss. The review finds clear links between contamination, bad sanitation, and illnesses like diarrhoea, cholera, typhoid, dengue, malaria, and leptospirosis. To assess these issues, researchers use household surveys, water testing, flood mapping, facility audits, and health assessments. Ultimately, the paper concludes that protecting health in informal areas requires combining reliable water supply, safe sanitation, good waste management, flood defense, and community monitoring.
caveats: Not stated whether primary data collection or statistical meta-analysis was performed beyond a narrative review.
Not stated how individual studies were selected or weighted in the synthesis.

title: Quantifying biodiversity and ecosystem service trade-offs to inform forest landscape management under changing conditions
headline: Forest legacies drive biodiversity and service trade-offs
bullets: Simulated long-term interactions between biodiversity and ecosystem services over 120 years.
Found that forest structure and past management heavily outweigh future changes.
Shows landscape management needs long-term structural strategies over short-term fixes.

plain.question: How do forest management and climate change affect biodiversity and nature benefits over time?
plain.method: Used long-term computer simulations of forest growth with many different management and climate scenarios.
plain.finding: Past forest management and age structure control biodiversity and service outcomes more than future changes.
plain.why: To show that improving nature benefits requires long-term structural strategies instead of quick fixes.

full.explainer: Forests provide many benefits and support biodiversity, but intensive management and climate change threaten them. This study looked at how biodiversity and multiple ecosystem services interact over a long time at the landscape scale. Researchers used a computer simulation model to test how different management choices, ownership types, disturbances, and climate changes affect a large temperate mountain region in Central Europe over a 120-year period. They found that differences in biodiversity and service levels were mainly caused by existing forest structure and past management legacies, such as the age of the trees and past zoning rules. Future shifts in management and climate disturbances had a smaller impact in this timeframe. The study discovered clear trade-offs between biodiversity and wood production, as well as between biodiversity and soil and water regulation or recreation. Opportunities to improve everything at once were rare. The main takeaway is that landscape multifunctionality is limited by long-term structural history, meaning real improvements require long-term structural plans.
caveats: Simulations are based on a specific temperate mountain region in Central Europe.
Future changes in management and climate only contributed marginally within the analyzed time horizon.

title: Syntropic infrastructure for regenerative urban metabolic reorganization in an Atlantic island city

plain.finding: Areas with less soil carbon were much hotter, and urban zones showed severe nature fragmentation.
plain.why: This helps cities use connected natural systems to stay cool, handle water, and protect life.

full.explainer: Cities often suffer from heat, poor water handling, and broken natural spaces. This paper suggests a new idea called syntropic infrastructure to fix these problems by reconnecting nature across the city. The researchers studied Santa Cruz de Tenerife to see how different environmental factors interact. They used computer mapping tools to look at nature links, surface temperatures, soil carbon, water runoff, and human access to nature, all set in a uniform grid. Their results showed that built-up areas have severe breaks in nature, and surface temperatures were much higher than in nearby vegetated areas. They found that places with more soil carbon had lower temperatures, while areas covered in hard surfaces were much hotter. The study suggests that planning with connected natural systems can help cool cities, manage water better, and make coastal and island areas more resilient to climate problems.
caveats: The study focuses on a specific coastal and island metropolitan system, Santa Cruz de Tenerife.

title: Vocabularies on Climate and Housing Justice from a Landfill in Bhalswa, New Delhi, India
headline: Climate and housing vulnerability near a Delhi landfill
bullets: Used a year-long ethnographic study of health histories with 15 waste-worker households.

plain.question: How do we talk about and solve the climate crisis where people already face severe housing inequality in the Global South?
plain.method: The researchers spent a year doing interviews and studying the health histories of 15 waste-worker households near a landfill.
plain.finding: Residents express climate and housing problems using local words like landfill, work, rent, and enduring, rather than science terms.
plain.why: It proves that housing and climate justice cannot be separated, and local vocabularies matter for political recognition.

full.explainer: Cities in the Global South face intense climate and environmental crises that worsen existing social and economic inequalities. This paper explores how to understand the climate crisis where people live with deep housing inequality. It looks at the case of waste workers living right next to the Bhalswa landfill in Delhi, India. These residents face unstable property rights, poor basic services, and constant dangers like landfill fires and polluted water, while their livelihoods depend on the landfill. The authors spent a year doing an ethnographic study, looking at health histories with 15 waste-worker households. They discovered that residents talk about climate and housing vulnerability using their own everyday vocabulary rather than technical climate science terms. By tracing four recurring Hindi words—referring to the landfill, work, rent, and enduring—the study shows how local terms form a unique register for experiencing climate change. The paper concludes that housing and climate justice must be handled together in the Global South, and respecting local vocabularies is a key form of political recognition.
caveats: The study is based on a small sample of 15 waste-worker households.
Not stated whether these findings apply outside of Delhi or other landfill communities.

plain.why: Climate changes can move disease-carrying insects into new regions.

full.explainer: Researchers studied Culex perexiguus, a mosquito typically found in hot and dry places like North Africa and the Middle East, because it can spread viruses like West Nile virus. In 2025, they collected 84 of these mosquitoes at 22 sites in Emilia-Romagna, northern Italy, and used DNA testing to confirm their identity. Comparing this with older data from 2009 showed that another mosquito species decreased at the same time, hinting at a northward shift in where these species can live. Ecological modeling showed that the mosquito's presence is linked to breeding habitats, and unusual weather in 2025 likely helped it survive there. Finding this warm-weather insect in a temperate area highlights how climate change is altering mosquito ranges, which poses new challenges for public health and disease monitoring.
caveats: The study links meteorological anomalies to the expansion, but does not prove direct causation.

title: Hidden in the desert: Community structure and temporal variation of scorpions (Arachnida: Scorpiones) in a protected area of Baja California Sur, Mexico
headline: Desert scorpion communities show seasonal variation
bullets: Sampled scorpion communities bimonthly for a year in a Mexican protected area
Found low species richness, with two species making up 79.3 percent of specimens

plain.question: How do scorpion populations change over time in a desert protected area?
plain.method: Collected scorpions every two months for a year in Mexico's desert.
plain.finding: Found few species, but many individuals, changing across seasons.
plain.why: Helps us understand desert ecology and supports future monitoring.

full.explainer: Researchers studied scorpion communities and population dynamics over one year in a protected desert area in Mexico. They used six bimonthly sampling events to collect data. They recorded four families, seven genera, and seven species, noting that the family Vaejovidae had the most species. Out of 729 collected scorpions, most were females, followed by males and juveniles. Two specific species dominated the total count, making up nearly 80 percent of all specimens collected. The data showed that species richness changed throughout the year, peaking in certain months, while total abundance reached its highest point in October. Diversity and evenness metrics varied by month, with some months showing an uneven distribution of species abundance. Multivariate analyses showed that the community composition shifted over time, likely due to seasonal weather changes and when different species are active. The authors state that these findings give baseline information for understanding scorpion dynamics in dry environments and help support future ecological monitoring.
caveats: Study is limited to a single protected area in Baja California Sur, Mexico.

title: Composite approach to quantifying regulating soil-based ecosystem services using multiple indicators
headline: Poland's soil-based ecosystem services are mostly low
bullets: Combined four regulating soil services and eleven indicators using geometric means.
Found that 84% of Polish agricultural soils have very low or low regulating status.

plain.question: How can we measure the benefits people get from soils across a whole country?
plain.method: They used maps, computer models, and math formulas to combine 11 different soil indicators into one score.
plain.finding: Most agricultural soils in Poland have very low or low capacity to provide these benefits.
plain.why: This helps leaders spot soil health problems and figure out where agriculture needs help.

full.explainer: Researchers tackled the challenge of mapping soil functions and soil-based ecosystem services, which are the benefits humans and the environment get from soils. Focusing on Poland, they created the first national-scale maps for regulating soil-based ecosystem services, which help with things like carbon storage, nutrient cycling, water regulation, and erosion control. They built a multi-indicator index using four soil services and eleven separate indicators, combining them with geometric means. For nutrients and carbon, they used digital soil mapping with a machine learning algorithm called quantile regression forest. For water regulation and erosion, they used other models. Their results revealed that regulating soil services in Poland's agricultural areas are quite low. Specifically, 84% of agricultural soils fell into very low or low status categories due to natural limits, while only 2% showed high status. The authors suggest this approach can be adapted for other regions and indicators worldwide.
caveats: Study focused nationally on Poland.
Not stated how non-agricultural soils performed.

title: Spatiotemporal characterization of heat waves in the semiarid region of Pernambuco, Brazil
headline: Surface heat waves grew significantly in Brazil's semiarid
bullets: Combined satellite land surface and air temperature data from 1994 to 2023.
Found surface heat waves increased significantly in frequency and duration.

plain.question: How did heat waves change over time in a dry region of Brazil?
plain.method: They used satellite images and climate data from 1994 to 2023.
plain.finding: Heat waves on the land surface became much more frequent and lasted longer.
plain.why: Air temperature alone misses how hot the land surface actually gets.

full.explainer: Heat waves are getting worse around the world, especially in dry areas where a lack of water makes warming even more intense. This study looked at how heat waves changed in a semiarid region of Pernambuco, Brazil, between 1994 and 2023. The researchers used a combination of satellite images to measure land surface temperature and climate data to measure air temperature. They looked at atmospheric events, surface events, and coupled events using a specific statistical threshold to measure their frequency, duration, and magnitude. They found that while air temperature heat waves did not show a major trend, surface heat waves became much more common, happening over 100 times per year with longer durations. Surface events also lasted longer and carried more heat than air events. This shows that looking only at air temperature misses a big part of the thermal stress happening on the ground. Combining satellite data with climate records provides a much more detailed picture of extreme heat in dry regions.
caveats: Not stated whether these findings apply to urban areas specifically.

title: Seeking coolness and shelter: behavioural responses of a large ungulate to severe weather conditions

plain.question: How do mountain animals change their behavior to deal with hot weather and rain?
plain.method: We tracked the GPS movements of 21 adult Alpine ibex in a park and compared them to weather data.
plain.finding: In warm weather, ibex moved to higher, shaded, and rugged spots. In rain, they moved downward.
plain.why: Animals need varied landscapes to survive climate change, which affects their ability to feed.

full.explainer:
Mountain environments face big challenges from climate change, like rising temperatures and changing rain. This study looks at how a large mountain animal, the Alpine ibex, changes its behavior to deal with bad weather. Researchers used high-resolution GPS tracking on 21 adult ibex in the Swiss National Park to see how they move and choose their habitats based on temperature and precipitation. 

The results show that ibex change their behavior depending on the weather. When it gets warm, they move to higher elevations, rugged ground, shaded spots, and less productive habitats to stay cool. They also walk further when it is warm. Instead of moving huge distances up mountains, they use small local patches for shade. When it rains, they move downwards to steeper terrain. These actions show that animals use landscape variety to handle weather, but trying to stay cool can get in the way of finding food. Keeping diverse landscapes connected is vital for their survival.

title: Instant urban climate modelling with AI: An interactive LEGO®-based workshop for public engagement with urban heat islands
headline: LEGO AI workshop teaches urban heat concepts
bullets: Built an interactive workshop using LEGO and AI temperature simulations for the public.
Found that over 85 percent of participants correctly identified urban heat and green cooling.
Shows how rapid data-driven models can improve public engagement with urban climate.

plain.question: How can we help people understand how cities trap heat?
plain.method: Children built mini cities with LEGO bricks, which AI scanned to instantly show heat maps.
plain.finding: Most children correctly saw that built areas are warmest and green areas are coolest.
plain.why: It proves fast tech tools can easily teach people about urban climate and cooling.

full.explainer: Urban heat islands are well studied, but their physical causes can be hard for non-experts to grasp. To bridge this gap, researchers created an interactive workshop that acts like a serious game. Participants use LEGO bricks to build miniature city layouts. These layouts are scanned and turned into land-cover maps, which feed into an artificial intelligence model to instantly simulate spatial temperatures during warm, low-wind nights. Run at public science events in Brussels from 2023 to 2025, the workshops mostly targeted children aged 7 to 12. Researchers gathered 400 post-workshop questionnaires across four editions in 2024 and 2025 to check learning and awareness. High percentages of participants gave correct answers: 86.2 percent knew built-up areas are warmest, 92.5 percent knew green areas are coolest, and 90.5 percent chose greener urban designs for cooling. Also, 77.1 percent said they learned something new. Statistical tests showed consistent results across different events.
caveats: Subgroup analyses by age, gender, living environment, and prior participation are purely descriptive.

full.explainer: When trying to restore plants in dry areas, wild animals eating the new plants is a big problem. Traditional fences and cages can be expensive and may harm the plants. This study tested a different idea: using reactive silicon, a substance plants naturally use for defense and health. The researchers looked at how silicon affected plant growth in a greenhouse and whether it protected plants from being eaten by wild herbivores in a small restoration field study. Before the plants faced any animals, those given silicon grew significantly taller and wider than the plants without it. However, when placed in the field, the silicon treatment did not reduce the amount of herbivory by wild animals. The authors conclude that while silicon does not stop animals from eating plants, applying it during the greenhouse stage can help boost early plant growth, which might help them survive better when finally planted outside.

title: Quantifying non-additive synergy in Blue–Green–grey Infrastructure for adaptive urban water resilience: A case study of Zixing City, China
headline: Combined infrastructure creates extra water benefits

plain.question: Does mixing different water infrastructure types create extra benefits?

full.explainer: This paper looks at how cities handle stormwater and water pollution by combining different types of water infrastructure, known as Blue-Green-Grey Infrastructure. The researchers studied Zixing City in China, which deals with rapid urbanization and stormwater issues. They used a computer modeling framework to test eight different scenarios, including baseline conditions, single measures, dual measures, and a fully integrated setup under different rainfall events. Instead of assuming that combining methods just adds their individual benefits together, the authors measured non-additive synergy—meaning they checked if the mix created extra benefits beyond the sum of its parts. Their results showed that fully integrated systems outperformed single and dual measures. The integrated setup generated positive synergistic gains for both runoff regulation and pollution reduction across all rainfall scenarios. Specifically, peak-flow reduction showed stable gains, while nutrient reduction achieved higher relative gains during low-intensity rainfall. The study concludes that these extra benefits happen because different infrastructure parts complement each other, such as source control, runoff routing, and downstream purification.

full.explainer: Finding small, low-intensity fires in wide satellite images is tricky because mixed pixels weaken the heat signals. Also, things like factories and solar panels can cause false alarms. To fix this, researchers created a new method using dual-scale thermal background adaptation and spatiotemporal semantic constraints. They tested it by detecting crop straw burning in China. The technique combines a wide look at thermal states with local neighborhood stats to adjust thresholds and catch weak fire candidates. It then uses historical heat data and proximity checks to filter out non-target heat sources while keeping real detections. Tests using satellite scenes and field surveys showed that fresh burn marks were present at 10 out of 12 checked sites. Furthermore, a transfer experiment reduced false detections near industrial facilities compared to official products. Overall, this framework helps screen for low-intensity fires and supports targeted field checks.

The researchers explain that these differences stem from the unique history, dominant plant species, and natural recovery of each site. Ultimately, the study demonstrates that established novel urban ecosystems can deliver significant carbon benefits. plain.question: How does city growth affect urban heat across Senegal?
plain.method: Used satellite images, maps, and machine learning to track building growth and ground temperatures from 2000 to 2024.
plain.finding: Cities grew massively, replacing farms and nature, which raised temperatures up to 49.0 degrees C in Touba.

full.explainer: As cities grow rapidly across West Africa, they trap more heat, creating urban heat islands. This study looks at eight major cities in Senegal over a 24-year period to see how city layouts, or urban morphology, affect temperatures. The researchers used several tools, including satellite data to track land changes and land surface temperatures, standard climate zone classifications, and a machine learning heat-stress map. They found that built-up areas expanded by 170 percent, mostly taking over farm land and natural savanna. This growth increased national land surface temperatures by 1.2 degrees Celsius, with some areas reaching 49 degrees. Compact building types experienced much higher heat stress than natural areas. Interestingly, the study discovered a dryland paradox: dense trees cool humid cities like Ziguinchor well, but do little in dry cities like Touba unless there is enough water. This gives a clear, open-source method for mapping heat that can help other dry or semi-arid cities plan better cooling strategies.
